title: Relays in the mountains
question: A drone flies a mountain valley. Where do the relays have to go to keep it in touch?

headlines.label: of the transit in touch, with relays on the summits
with relays on the valley floor
to the nearest relay at the worst moment
headlines.detail: close enough by range, hidden behind a ridge

summary: A drone crosses a mountain range at 80 m above the ground, and every relay has its own satellite backhaul, so the drone is in touch whenever it can reach any relay, directly or through another. Radio links are charged knife-edge diffraction loss for the worst ridge between the two ends, so line of sight decides coverage, not distance. With relays on the summits the drone stays in touch 81% of the way; the same flight with relays on the valley floor manages 60%. The last chart shows why: at the worst moment r3 was only 3.7 km away, inside radio range, but the ridge between them rises through the line of sight.

charts.caption: valley floor placement, longest outage: r3 was only 3.7 km away, inside radio range, but the ridge between them rises through the line of sight. At 900 MHz anything inside the first Fresnel zone costs diffraction loss.

method: Terrain is a sum of Gaussian peaks over 8 × 6 km. Links are 900 MHz free-space loss at 30 dBm with a 6 km hard range, minus single knife-edge diffraction (ITU-R P.526) over the worst obstruction on each path. The drone follows the terrain at 80 m and 25 m/s; relays sit on a 10 m mast; every link runs 500 ms keep-alives. Connected means any route to any relay, sampled every 200 ms over one transit, with the real wayfinder router on every node.
